title: Lior and the Interior
premise: Tamsin Blackwood, a piano tuner who reads houses through their radiators and pipes, is hired to prepare the condemned Lior House for its final inventory before demolition. Behind a wardrobe she finds a box of undelivered letters written by her estranged mother, Vera, to a man named Elias Lior — letters that reveal Tamsin was the reason Vera never sent them. As the demolition date closes in, Tamsin must decide whether the house's secrets belong to her or to the past, learning that power over memory is just another way of refusing to grieve. The novel ends on the morning of the wrecking ball: Tamsin stands in the empty house and says goodbye out loud — to her mother, to Elias, to herself — then walks out as the walls come down.
about_author: Tamsin Nystrom grew up above a funeral home in coastal Maine, where she learned early that houses keep accounts. She has worked as a piano tuner, an archivist, and a demolition-site surveyor, and writes about the strange intimacy between people and the buildings they abandon.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She arrives at Lior House for a pre-demolition survey, reading its failing radiators like a medical chart. Her practiced smile deflects the site manager's small talk. Emotional beat: competent isolation — a woman fluent in houses and mute with people.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Condemned Thing
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She catalogs rooms that hold decades of another family's life. A neighbor, Ruth, mentions the Lior family 'had a boarder once who left in a hurry.' Tamsin feels an unexplained chill. Beat: curiosity stirring beneath professional detachment.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Moving a wardrobe to check a radiator valve, she finds a cavity containing a shoebox of letters, all addressed to Elias Lior, all stamped, none mailed. The handwriting stops her cold: it is her mother's. Beat: shock; the past reaches through plaster.

chapters.title: Vera's Hand
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with letter excerpts. She reads the first three letters at night in her apartment — dated 1979–1981, tender, hopeful, addressed to a man Vera clearly loved. No mention of why they went unsent. Beat: hunger for a mother she never really knew.

chapters.title: The Boarder
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. In 1980, young Ruth watched Elias Lior take in a quiet woman named Vera as a lodger, and noticed how the house seemed to warm around them both. Beat: warmth shadowed by foreboding; the reader sees what Tamsin cannot.

chapters.title: What the Letters Withhold
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The letters grow strained — Vera writing around something, apologizing without naming it. Tamsin realizes the gap in dates matches her own birth year. She returns to the house seeking answers in its pipes. Beat: dread braided with need.

chapters.title: Elias's Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She tracks down Elias Lior's records: he died in 1996, alone, having lived in the house until the end. His obituary lists no family. Tamsin wonders if he ever knew about her. Beat: grief arriving sideways, for a stranger who might have been kin.

chapters.title: The Developer's Offer
chapters.summary: Site manager Dale's POV. Dale offers Tamsin a bonus to sign off early and hand over anything found on site — company policy claims artifacts. He is polite, reasonable, quietly menacing. Beat: institutional power flexing; the box becomes leverage.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She signs the survey but keeps the letters, lying smoothly with the smile that ends conversations — and hates how easily it comes. That night she drinks and rereads letter seven, where Vera writes 'I chose wrong, and the choosing made me.' Beat: guilt and defiance entwined.

chapters.title: Ruth Remembers
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, present day. Elderly Ruth tells Tamsin what she saw: Vera pregnant, Elias willing to claim the child, and Vera leaving anyway after a visit from her own father, who threatened to ruin Elias. Beat: the machinery of old power revealed — respectability as a weapon.

chapters.title: The Grandfather's Ledger
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Digging into family papers, she finds her grandfather's ledger: payments to Vera through the years, conditional on silence, ending only at his death. Her mother survived by being bought. Beat: fury and pity colliding; survival's price itemized.

chapters.title: Letter Twelve
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Letter twelve, the last, is unfinished: 'If you are reading this, I failed to be brave twice.' Tamsin understands Vera kept the letters as penance, never intending delivery. Beat: heartbreak reframed — cowardice as a lifelong wound, not a single act.

chapters.title: Dale Turns the Screw
chapters.summary: Dale's POV. Dale learns Tamsin removed items from the site and threatens legal action and blacklisting unless she surrenders them. He genuinely believes he is following procedure. Beat: banal corruption; the system needs no villain, only compliance.

chapters.title: The Smile Breaks
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Cornered, she tries her perfected deflection on Dale and watches it fail — he simply waits. For the first time in years she speaks plainly: these letters are hers, and she will not trade them. Beat: the mask cracks; voice found at cost.

chapters.title: House as Witness
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, lyrical interlude. Alone in Lior House overnight (she still holds keys), she tunes the last working piano and lets the radiators' hiss feel like the house answering. She asks aloud what Vera asked in the letters: whether love owed here was ever returned. Beat: communion; grief given a room.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth admits she told Vera's father where Vera was living — a girl's gossip that armed a tyrant. She has carried it fifty years. Tamsin chooses not to forgive instantly but to witness honestly. Beat: two survivors trading weight; forgiveness deferred, not denied.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The date moves up ten days; Dale's firm accelerates to cut off her access. Legal counsel confirms the letters are legally hers but the house will fall regardless. Beat: clock tightening; no institution will grant her the time she needs.

chapters.title: What Tamsin Owes
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She confronts her own pattern: jobs ended, friendships starved, every goodbye pre-empted by departure. Vera's unsent letters are her inheritance, and she has been mailing nothing herself. Beat: recognition; the theme turns inward.

chapters.title: Deliveries
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She mails copies of the letters to Elias's surviving grandniece, gives Ruth the one addressed to 'the neighbor girl,' and keeps only letter twelve. Each envelope is a small act of courage she rehearses at the post office counter. Beat: restitution; grief converted into motion.

chapters.title: The Last Walkthrough
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Final inspection with Dale watching. She signs everything, returns the keys, and asks for five minutes alone. He grants it — procedure, for once, serving grace. Beat: threshold; the house reduced to minutes.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the emptied parlor she speaks to Vera, to Elias, to the child her mother couldn't keep brave — saying goodbye properly, naming what was taken and what was chosen. She leaves letter twelve open on the floor for the house to read first. Beat: climax and release; voice fully claimed.

chapters.title: After the Walls
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, weeks later. From a bench she watches the wrecking ball fall, then doesn't stay for the dust. She books a train to visit Ruth weekly, takes a new tuning job, and answers her phone when it rings. Beat: resolution; survival redefined as staying, speaking, remaining reachable.
